zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Secondary lexical reference: *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html License: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ The BnF scan remains the primary evidence; review corrections and chosen readings are distinguished in the line notes.

lines.note: Continues the preceding Japanese quotation: the adorned palace rises into the clouds. The mark over u is a caron in this impression; the printed cǔden is retained rather than substituting a modern palace-name spelling.
The upright citation label Taif. introduces book 37; the Portuguese translation begins with the houses of great lords. The label is distinct from the italic bibliographical apparatus.
Continues the description of the great lords' houses as bright and splendid. The following conjunction carries the translation onto the next physical row.

runs.text: altas que ſe hião às nuuẽs.

lines.note: Completes the architectural image: the houses were so high that they reached the clouds. The historical hião and abbreviated nuuẽs are not modernized.
Rocai denotes rowing implements, glossed as oars and paddles. The unusual Portuguese pangayos is visible and does not need replacement by a modern term.
Rôcutaxi denotes letting someone die through prolonged imprisonment. The scan restores the initial R and the x of Deixar; mui- continues as muito below.
Completes muito tempo no carcere: keeping the person in prison for a long time. This is the continuation of Rôcutaxi, not a separate definition.

runs.text: Couſa de ſeis quinas, ou cantos.

lines.note: Roccacu is a six-cornered or six-angled object. The doubled consonant belongs to the Japanese form; quinas and cantos provide mutually reinforcing Portuguese glosses.
The adjectival form Roccacuna has the same six-cornered meaning. Its initial R is upright with a decorative tail, not an isolated italic letter.
Roccacuni is the corresponding adverbial form, identified by italic Adu. The Japanese headword remains entirely upright.

Roccon names six faculties in the Japanese classification. The Portuguese says six senses, not a compound word Seisſentidos; the explanation continues with the five external senses and a common faculty.

runs.text: ſ, os cinco exteriores, & o ſentido comum. Vt,

lines.note: Specifies five external senses and the common sense or mental faculty. The printed abbreviation ſ is preserved, and Vt introduces the following enumeration.

Enumerates the six faculties through their Japanese names: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The final upright I names the mental faculty, not the alternative marker l. The locally mixed type of xin is retained rather than regularized; its precise font boundary remains a nonblocking typography caveat.
Rôchô is a bird in a cage, explicitly paraphrased by Cagono tori. The Portuguese bird-word is restored from the damaged OCR and continues with gayola on the next row.
Completes the cage definition. Gayola is the printed historical Portuguese spelling; the short row remains a separate physical line.
The first Rôchǔ is the interior of a tower or bastion, as Yagurano vchi makes clear. The Portuguese word balluarte is divided across the line end; it is not a full stop after balluar.
Completes balluarte and adds a small tower as an alternative. The diminutive torrinha clarifies the architectural, rather than prison, sense of this entry.
The next Rôchǔ concerns being inside a prison, paraphrased by Rôno vchi. This is a separate homophonous entry from the tower-interior sense above.
Completes the prison definition with carcere. The one-word row belongs to the preceding Rôchǔ entry.
Rochǔ is the middle of the road or journey, explained by Michi naca. The absence of a long-vowel mark on the first o distinguishes the printed form from the preceding entries.
Rǒcô means the fruit or merit of labor. The middle consonant is c, not OCR e, and the two o marks differ in the printed headword.
Rǒcôuo tçumu means accumulating meritorious service. The object ending is uo, not OCR un; a visible paragraph sign introduces the example and the Portuguese has no comma after Ajuntar.
Completes the translation as gathering services and merits through labor. It carries on the same example rather than introducing another Japanese expression.

Rôcǒ denotes a crossroads or road junction, explained by Chimata and Michitçuji. The initial R is restored; the faint first vowel mark is provisionally read ô, with secondary support from the supplied NINJAL index, entry 212a12. Its worn direction remains uncertain; the final caron and Encru- are clear.

runs.text: zilhada, ou caminho por onde todos paßão.

lines.note: Completes encruzilhada and describes a route along which everyone passes. The historical ß form in paßão is retained; caminho begins with a lowercase c in the scan.
Rôcocu is a timepiece, with Toqei as its Japanese equivalent. The Portuguese gives a sand clock as one example; the initial vowel mark and contracted darea are retained as printed.
Adds water clocks and other kinds to the preceding description of timepieces. Agoa is a continuation of the Portuguese list, not an independent entry.
Rocu is wealth or a bestowed treasure, paraphrased with Tamamono and Tacara. The scan supports Riquezas, correcting the OCR's misplaced j.
The two Japanese verbs describe accumulating or storing wealth. The alternative marker l is preserved, and Ajun- continues as Ajuntar below.
Completes the explanation: gathering much wealth in order to give it. The separation pera dar is visible and should not be collapsed into one word.
This Rǒcu is toil and suffering, paraphrased as Xinrǒ curuximi. The scan supplies the mark on Xinrǒ; the Portuguese list continues with fatigue.
Completes the labor-and-suffering definition by adding fatigue. The short Portuguese continuation remains on its own physical row.
A separate Rǒcu concerns the pains of old age. Voino curuximi means the suffering of aging; the OCR's Vonuo cunuximi obscured both the possessive construction and the word for suffering.
Completes the description of troubles or afflictions arising from old age. This limits the preceding Rǒcu more specifically than the general labor sense.

Rocuchicu introduces a six-animal classification, beginning with cattle, sheep, and dogs. The Japanese enumeration follows i and is not an ordinary Portuguese sentence containing italicized Japanese words.
Completes the Japanese list with horse, domestic fowl, and young boar. The Portuguese translation begins with ox or cow; its final o- belongs to ovelha on the following row.

runs.text: uelha, cão, caualo, gallo, filho de porco mõtes.

lines.note: Completes the animal list as sheep, dog, horse, cock, and offspring of a wild boar. The source's specific boar wording is retained rather than generalized silently to pig.

runs.text: Rocudai. i, Giſui, qua, fǔ, cǔ, xiqi.

lines.note: Rocudai names six elements. Giſui visibly runs earth and water together before fire, wind, space, and consciousness; no editorial comma is inserted inside that printed token. The marks over fǔ and cǔ are carons.

runs.text: ra, agoa, fogo, vento, & mais duas ſuſtã-

lines.note: Completes Terra and lists earth, water, fire, and wind, then introduces two further substances. The abbreviated and divided ſuſtã- continues below without expansion.
Completes the six-element gloss with two invisible substances. The Portuguese characterization is preserved as the dictionary's explanation, not replaced by modern technical terminology.

runs.text: Rocudǒ. Mutçuno michi. i, Gigocu, gaqi,

lines.note: Rocudǒ means six paths or realms; Mutçuno michi supplies that Japanese explanation. The first realm-names are Gigocu and gaqi, and the initial M corrects OCR Nutçuno.
Continues the realm list with animals, asuras, humans, and celestial beings. The visible den is retained rather than regularized to expected ten; the Portuguese calls all six infernos.

runs.text: aßi chamados que os gẽtios imaginão auer neſta

lines.note: Continues the dictionary's account of realms that non-Christians believe to exist. The religious framing belongs to the historical gloss; both ß and the abbreviated gẽtios are preserved.
Completes the clause by locating those realms in the present life. The unusual scope of the Portuguese explanation is copied, not doctrinally corrected.
Rocufaramit names six perfections, here explained as qualities or gifts of the soul. The scan restores qualidades; the final t is the printed Japanese checked ending, not an omitted syllable.
Completes dalma and attributes the six qualities to Buddhist teaching. Buppò is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is set upright in this impression.
Rocugu denotes armor covering the whole body. The final Ro- begins an example continued at the top of the next column; it is body text, not a catchword.
Joins the preceding column's Ro- to form Rocugu xite, being fully armored. The opening fragment is correctly assigned to this physical row and is not an independent headword.

runs.text: Terra, ou caminho por terra. Vt,

lines.note: Rocugi means land or a route by land. Vt introduces examples with verbs of going and walking on the next row.
The example means to go or walk by land. The alternative verb ayumu follows l; Portuguese caminhar is divided after cami-.
Completes caminhar por terra. The letter is h, not the OCR's b, and the row finishes the overland-travel example.

runs.text: Certo comer que ſe faz cõ

lines.note: Rocugiô is a food prepared with dried tofu. Tofus is an upright Japanese food-name within a Portuguese explanation, and a comma follows ſecos in the scan.
Adds that the tofu used for this preparation is hard as well as dry. The short continuation qualifies the ingredient in the preceding row.
Rocu-i combines wealth and rank, explicitly paraphrased by Tacara and curai. The internal hyphen is printed headword evidence; the Portuguese dignidades continues below.
Completes dignidades, the rank or honor component of Rocu-i. This fragment is not to be joined physically to the preceding row in the returned transcription.
Rocuna describes something level, illustrated by a level road. Praina is the historical Portuguese form and is not normalized to plana.

runs.text: Caminho praino, & raſo. Itẽ, Couſa direita.

lines.note: Translates the example as a level, flat road and adds the sense straight or upright. The abbreviated Itẽ introduces that additional meaning.
Rocuni is the adverbial counterpart of Rocuna. The faint middle c is retained from the visible headword rather than treating the damaged impression as a missing letter.
Rocuqiǔ is a deerskin garment, paraphrased by Canoxixino cauagoromo. The Portuguese word vestido is divided at the edge; the OCR's ß is not supported here.

runs.text: do de pelle de veado. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the deerskin definition and starts an example about warding off cold. Canuo is the object of the verb continued below, not another garment name.

runs.text: O vestido de pelle de veado defẽ-

lines.note: The example says that the deerskin garment wards off cold. The damaged a after ſ retains a lower bowl and lacks an i dot, supporting ſayeguiru rather than the OCR ſiyeguiru. The Portuguese defẽ- continues with its abbreviation tilde across the line break.
Completes the translation as protection from cold. The row belongs to the same deerskin example and does not start a new sense.

runs.text: Pião de dentro do ſõbreiro do ſol.

lines.note: This Rocuro is the central internal fitting of a parasol. The scan reads Pião, not OCR Pũão; the tilde in ſõbreiro is also retained on its printed vowel.
The second Rocuro is a craftsman's lathe. The paragraph sign introduces an example whose headword fragment Rocu- continues as roni below; the ornamental R remains upright.
Completes Rocuroni caqete fiqu, making an object on a lathe. Both the Japanese phrase and Portuguese translation concern turning work.
Rocuro fiqi is a worker who uses a lathe, a turner. The printed space between Rocuro and fiqi is preserved.
Rocuroxi gives another name for the same turner. Idem refers to the immediately preceding occupational entry.
Rocuſuinǒ denotes a water strainer, directly explained by Mizucoxi. The visible long ſ is kept rather than importing the normalized s from a lexical index.
Rǒcut is advanced, enfeebled old age. The final Japanese t is a checked ending and is preserved without an added vowel.
The example states that the speaker has become thoroughly old. The scan restores both the paragraph sign and the final t of Rǒcut, correcting the OCR's Rǒcuc.

runs.text: Moços de ſeruiço que ſeruem à gẽ-

lines.note: Rocuxacu identifies household servants serving townspeople. The Portuguese gẽ- is an abbreviated word fragment continued as gente on the next row.

runs.text: te dos Machis dentro de caſa.

lines.note: Completes the servants' duties as service inside the houses of people in the Machis, or towns. Machis is a Japanese place-category embedded in Portuguese and is flagged for whole-word typeface review.

Rocuxin means six kinds of close kin, paraphrased as Mutçuno xitaximi. The final Japanese vowel is i, not the OCR's italic ũ; the Portuguese parentes continues as parentescos without a visible line-end hyphen.

runs.text: cos de pay, mãy, irmão maior, de irmão me-

lines.note: Completes parentescos and lists father, mother, elder brother, and the beginning of younger brother. The apparent repetition de before irmão is retained from the print.
Completes menor and adds wife and children to the six kinship categories. The source's molher spelling is preserved.

runs.text: Seis noticias, que ſe alcanção por

lines.note: Rocuxiqi concerns six forms of awareness or cognition. Noticias is used here in the knowledge sense, as the following explanation by the senses makes clear.
Completes the description of knowledge acquired through six inner senses. The wording is the historical Portuguese account and is not rewritten to conform to modern terminology.

runs.text: Certo mineral de cor verde que ſerue

lines.note: Rocuxǒ is a green mineral used as a coloring material. The identification remains at the source's level without asserting a particular modern chemical composition.
Completes the mineral definition by stating its use in pigments or paints. The row is a short but genuine body-text continuation.

Rocuxu is equated with Rocudǒ, the six realms already described in the first column. The Portuguese word for hells carries an abbreviation mark over its initial i; the religious description is preserved as printed.
Rǒdô refers to soldiers who are retainers of a lord. The abbreviated dalgũ is copied without expansion.

runs.text: Lugar dos remos, quando ſe rema.

lines.note: Rodoco is the place or fitting for the oars when rowing. The gloss describes its function without specifying a modern boat-part identification.
Rǒfan combines weariness and illness, as Tçucare vazzurǒ explains. The headword's faint vowel mark is retained as a caron after comparison with the other aging and labor entries.
Completes the gloss as weakness from illness. The closing S. is an upright written-register label, separate from the italic Portuguese explanation.
Rǒfei is an old soldier, explicitly paraphrased by Voitaru tçuuamono. The final adjective of the Portuguese gloss is carried onto the next row.
Completes Soldado ja velho. This one-word continuation belongs to the old-soldier entry.
Rofen means beside the hearth, explained by Irorino fotori. The final tilde belongs to o in fogaõ in this impression, not to the preceding a.
Rǒfit literally invokes an old brush and is glossed as an old scribe, then an old person's handwriting. The abbreviated Itẽ introduces the second sense.
Completes Letra de velho, the handwriting sense of Rǒfit. It is not part of the following old-man entry.
Rǒfu is an old man, paraphrased by Voita votto. This is distinct from the following father-related homophone.
A second Rǒfu means an aged father; Melius recommends Rǒbu instead. The scan reads f, not OCR r, in the headword, and the recommended Japanese form is upright.
Completes Pay velho, an old father. It belongs to the Melius entry immediately above.
Rǒgacu is study undertaken in old age. The historical separation de pois is visible and retained.
Rǒgan means the eyes of an old person, explicitly paraphrased by Voino manaco. The Portuguese reads Olhos rather than OCR Olhas; the Rogan beneath it is a separate catchword for the next page.
The far-right Rogan. anticipates the opening headword of f424. It is normal-sized roman catchword text, not display text or a further dictionary entry.
